sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Hēlios** (*helios*) — Sun (from ἕλος) — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Sun, Sight, Oaths". The name means "Sun (from ἕλος)"[^1].

Hēlios is the sun itself: a god who sees everything and drives his blazing chariot across the sky each day. **Nothing hidden escapes him**, and mortals and gods alike swear oaths by his light.[^2]

PÚNYCODEX restores the name as **Hēlios** and serves its temple at [hēlios.com](https://xn--hlios-iza.com). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *helios* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1843.
Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.
Wörterbuch der griechischen Eigennamen, 3rd ed., 1863.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Greek as **Ἥλιος**. Etymologically it means "Sun (from ἕλος)"[^1].

The reconstructed proto-form is *seh₂wol-* (proto-indo-european, "sun"). From Ἥλιος "sun", cognate with Latin sol, English sun. The solar charioteer.

Cognate forms across related languages:

- **sol** (latin) — The sun
- **Sūrya** (sanskrit) — Vedic sun god

The ASCII form *helios* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Hēlios** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **h** → **H** — Rough breathing
- **e** → **ē** — Eta: long epsilon
- **l** → **l** — Lambda
- **i** → **i** — Short iota
- **o** → **o** — Short omicron
- **s** → **s** — Sigma

The project holds the domain **hēlios.com** (xn--hlios-iza.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1843.
Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/hɛ́.li.os/** — Attic Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Hē-** — Short epsilon with rough breathing, pitched high — the first flash of dawn.
- **-li-** — Lambda plus short iota — the bright, liquid center of the name.
- **-os** — Short omicron-sigma — the masculine ending that names him.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'HAY-lee-oss' — the first syllable rises like the sun; the rest is bright and clear.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **PIE** — *sóh₂wl̥ 'sun' — root of Greek ἥλιος, Latin sol, English 'sun'
- **Greek** — ἕλιξ (helix), possibly associated by folk etymology with the sun's turning course
- **Mycenaean** — e-u-me-ne / *Heliwerges, possible theophoric name

Hēlios is Tier 2 because the Greek Ἥλιος preserves stress (acute on the first epsilon) but no long vowel. The name is built on the same root as English 'sun' and Latin 'sol,' one of the most ancient theonyms in the Indo-European family.

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1843.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in Greek as **Ἥλιος** — Greek alphabet (Classical / Attic), attested Ancient Greek, c. 8th century BCE – present, in Greece and the Greek-speaking Mediterranean. The script is written left-to-right.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *Hēlios* (Greek alphabet with polytonic accents), giving the normalized reading /hɛːˈli.os/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- The Greek form Ἥλιος is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
- Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
- Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
- The Unicode restoration Hēlios encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

sources.citation: Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek.
Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque.
Liddell-Scott-Jones (LSJ).
Wörterbuch der griechischen Eigennamen, 3rd ed., 1863.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Hēlios is the sun itself: a god who sees everything and drives his blazing chariot across the sky each day. **Nothing hidden escapes him**, and mortals and gods alike swear oaths by his light.[^1]

### The Chariot of the Sun

He rises from Oceanus in the east, crosses the sky, and descends into the western sea.

### All-Seeing Witness

He sees everything on earth; oaths sworn in his name are binding because he cannot be deceived.

### Revealer of Secrets

He exposed Aphrodítē's affair with Árēs to Hēphaistos; he told Demeter of Persephone's abduction.

### Healer and Life-Giver

His warmth makes crops grow and bodies live; his withdrawal is winter and death.

sources.citation: Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Hēlios concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **Chariot** — The vehicle that carries the sun across the sky
- **Winged sun disk** — The sun as a flying radiant power
- **Crown of rays** — The projecting beams of light
- **Horse** — The horses of his chariot, often named Pyrois, Eous, Aethon, and Phlegon
- **Whip** — His control over the solar horses
- **Globe or disk** — The sun itself

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Hēlios's myths all depend on his unique vantage point: **he sees everything**. This makes him a witness, a revealer, and occasionally a victim of his own children's ambition.[^1]

### Across the Sky and Through Oceanus (The Daily Journey)

Each dawn Hēlios rises from Oceanus in the east, drawn by four horses in a chariot of fire. At midday he sees the entire world spread below him. In the evening he sinks into the western Ocean, where he is received in a golden cup and conveyed back to the east. The Homeric *Hymn to Helios* (1–14) describes this journey as the source of all life and growth.[^2]

### The Exposure of Ares and Aphrodite (The Witness)

In *Odyssey* 8.266–366, Hēlios sees Árēs and Aphrodítē committing adultery in Hēphaistos's house and reports it to the cuckolded smith. Hēphaistos then traps the lovers in a net. The episode shows that Hēlios is not merely a celestial body but a moral witness; nothing done in daylight is hidden from him.

### Phaethon and the Scorched Earth (The Son)

Phaethon, son of Hēlios and the nymph Clymene, begged to drive the solar chariot. Hēlios reluctantly agreed, but Phaethon could not control the horses. He scorched the earth, creating the deserts of Africa, until Zeüs struck him down with a thunderbolt. The myth is a warning against claiming divine power without divine skill; it also explains the origin of the Sahara.

### Helios and the Cattle of Thrinacia (The Island)

In the *Odyssey* (12.127–141), Hēlios pastures his sacred cattle on the island of Thrinacia. Odysseus's crew, despite warnings, slaughter and eat the cattle. Hēlios demands vengeance and threatens to shine among the dead; Zeüs destroys Odysseus's ship with a thunderbolt. The sun god's cattle are the cosmos's property, and their violation brings universal retribution.

sources.citation: Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.
Wörterbuch der griechischen Eigennamen, 3rd ed., 1863.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The Romans identified Hēlios with Sol, though Apollo increasingly absorbed solar attributes in both Greek and Roman religion. The emperor Aurelian made Sol Invictus the official patron of the Roman Empire in 274 CE, and the cult influenced the dating of Christmas. In Hellenistic Egypt, Hēlios was syncretized with Osiris and with the Egyptian sun god Ra as a universal deity. Neoplatonists saw Hēlios as the visible image of the One. The heliocentric model of Copernicus gave Hēlios's name a scientific afterlife: the sun, not the earth, is the center.[^1]

Kindred figures in the PÚNYCODEX cross-tradition index include [[apollon|Apóllōn]], [[surya|Sūrya]], [[dazhbog|Dažbog]], [[huitzilopochtli|Huitzilopōchtli]], [[ra|Rꜥ]], and [[shamash|Šamaš]], each linked through sun / light.

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1843.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Hēlios is the namesake of heliocentrism, helium, and countless words for sunlight. The Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, was a giant statue of Hēlios. His crown of rays influenced depictions of Christ as 'Sol Invictus' and the halo in Christian art. In modern culture, the sun god remains a symbol of clarity, revelation, and dangerous power. Restoring *Hēlios* restores the original Greek name of the star that makes life possible.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1843.

Lindos: colossal dedication by Chares (predecessor to the Colossus of Rhodes); Rhodes: Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders.

sections.label: Homeric Hymns
sections.body:
Hēlios has one short hymn, the thirty-first of the collection: nineteen lines calling on the Muse to sing 'of Hēlios, whom the ox-eyed Euryphaessa bore to the son of Earth and starry Heaven' — Hyperion — and describing how he yokes his horses at dawn and drives them until evening, looking down upon the grain-giving earth. Like the other late miniature hymns to celestial powers (Hymns 8 and 32), it is a liturgical prelude rather than a narrative.[^1]

His epic presence is older and larger. Hesiod makes him the child of Hyperion and Theia, brother of Selene and Eos (*Theogony* 371–374).[^2] The *Odyssey* gives him his great scenes: the island Thrinacia with the sacred cattle (Book 12) and his role as the all-seeing informer who exposes what daylight sees.[^3]

sources.citation: Homeric Hymn 31, To Helios.
Hesiod, Theogony 371–374.
Homer, Odyssey 8 and 12.

sections.label: Epithets & Epicleses
sections.body:
His titles track his one defining quality: total visibility.

- **Ὑπεριονίδης** (*Hyperionidēs*) — 'son of Hyperion,' Homer's and Hesiod's regular title; Homer often calls him simply Hyperiōn.[^1]
- **Πανόπτης** (*panoptēs*) — 'all-seeing,' the title later poetry and the Orphic hymn to Hēlios fasten on him; the Iliad already invokes 'Hēlios, who seest all things and hearest all things.'[^2]
- **Τιτάν** (*Titan*) — in later Greek and Latin poetry the sun is the Titan par excellence, a title that passed into Roman Sol.[^3]
- **Ἀνίκητος** (*anikētos*) — 'unconquered,' his late-antique cult title, the Greek of Sol Invictus, stamped on imperial coinage from the third century CE.[^3]

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad and Odyssey; Hesiod, Theogony 371–374.
Homer, Iliad 3.276–277; Orphic Hymn 8, To Helios.
OCD, s.v. Sol; late antique coinage of Aurelian and Constantine I.

sections.label: Oracle & Cult Sites
sections.body:
Despite being the god who sees everything, Hēlios kept no oracular seat in mainland Greece; prophecy belonged to Apóllōn, and the sun's witness was invoked in oaths rather than consulted.[^1]

His real cult geography:

- **Rhodes** — the island was his portion, awarded while he was absent at the division of the world; Pindar's *Olympian* 7 tells the myth, and the Rhodians honored him as chief god with the quadrennial Halieia.[^2]
- **Lindos (Rhodes)** — his sanctuary beside Athena's on the acropolis; the Colossus's sculptor, Chares, was a Lindian.[^3]
- **Corinth** — a temple of Hēlios with a bronze image stood on the road up to Acrocorinth.[^4]

Divination did attach to him in the Greek Magical Papyri of Roman Egypt, where the all-seeing sun is conjured for revelations — a late, private counterpart to the public oracle he never had.[^5]

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 3.276–277 (oath by the all-seeing sun).
Pindar, Olympian 7 (Helios and Rhodes).
Pliny the Elder, Natural History 34.41 (Chares of Lindos).
Pausanias, Description of Greece 2.4 (Corinth).
Greek Magical Papyri (solar invocation spells).

sections.label: Iconography
sections.body:
Hēlios's type is fixed by one feature: the **radiate crown**. He is a beardless youth with rays springing from his head — a formula appearing on Rhodian coinage from the fifth century BCE and, as the facing radiate head, one of the most widespread coin images of the Hellenistic world.[^1]

His second great image is the **chariot**: four horses rising from the sea at dawn, beloved of Attic vase painters and architectural sculpture — the horses of Hēlios and the sinking chariot of Selene frame the two corners of the Parthenon's east pediment.[^2]

The **Colossus of Rhodes** (c. 280 BCE, by Chares of Lindos), some thirty metres of bronze, stood as his monumental portrait until the earthquake of 226 BCE; Pliny preserves its measurements and its fame among the Seven Wonders.[^3] Rome's Sol Invictus on the coins of Aurelian and Constantine is the direct heir of the Rhodian type.[^1]

sources.citation: Lexicon Iconographicum Mythologiae Classicae (LIMC), s.v. Helios.
A. Stewart, Greek Sculpture: An Exploration (1990) (the Parthenon pediments).
Pliny the Elder, Natural History 34.41 (the Colossus).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Hēlios is the god of total visibility. He cannot be bargained with or hidden from. In an age of surveillance, we have made our own Hēlios — satellites, cameras, data trails — but without the moral clarity the god represented. For the Greeks, the sun's witness was sacred; for us, visibility is often exploitative.

The restoration of Hēlios's name is a reminder that light is not neutral. It reveals, but it also exposes. The sun sees everything, and what it sees cannot be undone.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1843.
